summary: How the lungs and airways grow out of the foregut, which tissues come from endoderm and which from mesoderm, and the five stages of lung development. Exam questions tie each step to what goes wrong: tracheoesophageal fistula, surfactant deficiency in preterm infants, and pulmonary hypoplasia.

points: In week 4 the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) grows out of the ventral wall of the foregut.
Endoderm forms the lining epithelium of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, plus the airway glands.
Splanchnic mesoderm around the bud forms the cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, and visceral pleura.
Laryngeal cartilages and muscles come from the mesenchyme of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6.
The bud splits into two primary bronchial buds in week 5; the right gives 3 secondary bronchi and the left gives 2, which sets up 3 lobes on the right and 2 on the left.
Tracheoesophageal ridges grow in from each side and fuse into the tracheoesophageal septum.
The septum divides the foregut into the trachea in front and the esophagus behind.
Faulty or incomplete septation gives tracheoesophageal fistula, often with esophageal atresia.
Most common form (about 85 percent): the upper esophagus ends blindly and the lower esophagus connects to the trachea.
Clues: polyhydramnios, drooling, choking or cyanosis with the first feed, a feeding tube that coils in the upper pouch, and a gas-filled stomach.
H-type fistula (no atresia) shows up later as recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
Often part of VACTERL association.
Embryonic (about weeks 4 to 7): lung bud, bronchial buds, lobes and segments.
Pseudoglandular (about weeks 5 to 16): branching down to terminal bronchioles; no gas exchange possible.
Canalicular (about weeks 16 to 26): respiratory bronchioles form and capillaries grow close to the airways.
Survival with intensive support first becomes possible near the end of the canalicular stage (about weeks 24 to 26), once these thin gas exchange units exist.
Saccular (about week 26 to birth): terminal sacs with type I and type II pneumocytes; the blood-air barrier thins.
Alveolar (late fetal life to about 8 years): true alveoli form; most alveoli are added after birth.
Type II pneumocytes begin making surfactant in the second trimester; levels become adequate at about week 35.
Main surfactant lipid: dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin).
An amniotic lecithin to sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio above 2 indicates mature fetal lungs.
Fetal cortisol speeds surfactant production; fetal hyperinsulinemia from maternal diabetes delays it.
Too little surfactant at birth causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
Normal lung growth needs amniotic fluid in the airways, fetal breathing movements, and room in the chest.
Oligohydramnios (bilateral renal agenesis, urinary obstruction, early membrane rupture) leaves the lungs small: Potter sequence with flat face, limb deformities, and hypoplastic lungs.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: a pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close, usually the left posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect.
Gut herniates into the chest and compresses the developing lung; the same side is worst, but the other lung can also be small.
Either cause gives respiratory failure at birth with pulmonary hypertension; diaphragmatic hernia also shows a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest.

tricks.label: Every Pulmonologist Can See Alveoli
tricks.text: Embryonic, Pseudoglandular, Canalicular, Saccular, Alveolar: the five stages in order.

tricks.label: Lining versus wall
tricks.text: Anything that lines the airway or secretes (epithelium, glands) is endoderm. Anything that holds it up or squeezes it (cartilage, muscle, connective tissue) is splanchnic mesoderm.

tricks.label: Canals before sacs
tricks.text: Canalicular means the canals for blood vessels arrive. Without capillaries next to the airways there is nothing to exchange gas with, which is why viability starts at the end of this stage.

highYield: The lung bud comes off the ventral foregut in week 4.
Most common tracheoesophageal fistula: blind upper esophageal pouch with a fistula from trachea to lower esophagus.
Polyhydramnios plus choking with the first feed and a coiled feeding tube means esophageal atresia.
L/S ratio above 2 means mature fetal lungs.
Viability begins near the end of the canalicular stage, about weeks 24 to 26.
Oligohydramnios from renal agenesis causes pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence).
Bochdalek hernia is usually left-sided and causes hypoplasia of the lung on that side.
Maternal diabetes delays surfactant production by raising fetal insulin.
pitfalls: Polyhydramnios goes with esophageal atresia (fetus cannot swallow); oligohydramnios goes with renal agenesis and pulmonary hypoplasia.
Surfactant production begins in the second trimester, yet adequate levels arrive only around week 35; a 28-week infant has some type II cells but not enough surfactant.
An H-type fistula has no atresia, so the infant feeds at first and presents later with repeated aspiration pneumonia.
Most alveoli form after birth; the alveolar stage continues into childhood.

dumps.p: Draw a timeline from week 4 of development to age 8. Mark each stage of lung development, what forms in it, and the point where a preterm infant can first survive with support.
l: Lung bud from ventral foregut in week 4
Pseudoglandular: branching to terminal bronchioles, no gas exchange
Canalicular: respiratory bronchioles and capillaries
Viability near weeks 24 to 26
Saccular: terminal sacs, type I and II pneumocytes
Surfactant adequate about week 35, L/S above 2
Alveolar stage continues to about age 8

Lower esophagus connects to the trachea

summary: The microscopic structure of the airway from nose to alveolus: how the lining epithelium changes along the way, what each cell type does, and what makes up the thin barrier where gas crosses. Exam questions link these cells to smoking damage, ciliary defects, impaired diffusion, and laryngeal cancer.

points: Trachea and bronchi: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
Larger bronchioles: ciliated simple columnar, with goblet cells thinning out.
Terminal bronchioles: simple cuboidal, ciliated, with many club cells and no goblet cells.
Respiratory bronchioles: cuboidal epithelium interrupted by alveoli opening off the wall.
Alveoli: type I and type II pneumocytes.
True vocal folds and oropharynx: nonkeratinized stratified squamous, which stands up to friction.
Trachea has C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings with the trachealis muscle behind; bronchi have irregular cartilage plates.
Bronchi have submucosal seromucous glands and goblet cells; bronchioles have neither cartilage nor glands.
Bronchioles have relatively more smooth muscle, so they narrow strongly in asthma.
Without cartilage, bronchioles stay open through smooth muscle tone and radial traction from the elastic alveolar walls attached around them.
Loss of that alveolar tethering (emphysema) lets bronchioles collapse on expiration and trap air.
Type I pneumocytes: thin squamous cells covering about 95 percent of the alveolar surface; they form the gas exchange surface.
Type II pneumocytes: cuboidal cells with lamellar bodies; they secrete surfactant and divide to replace type I cells after injury.
Club cells: nonciliated dome-shaped cells in bronchioles; they secrete protective proteins, detoxify inhaled toxins with cytochrome P450, and act as progenitor cells.
Alveolar macrophages (dust cells): come from blood monocytes and clear particles and microbes; hemosiderin-filled ones are called heart failure cells.
Goblet cells and submucosal glands make the mucus layer.
Cilia beat toward the pharynx and carry the mucus blanket and trapped particles up and out.
Each cilium has a 9 plus 2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets around two central microtubules.
Dynein arms on the doublets use ATP to slide the doublets past each other, which bends the cilium.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome): defective dynein arms give sinusitis, bronchiectasis, infertility, and situs inversus in about half.
Smoking replaces ciliated columnar epithelium with stratified squamous epithelium (squamous metaplasia), which has no cilia.
Smoking also enlarges submucosal glands and adds goblet cells, so more mucus is made while less is cleared.
Retained mucus lets bacteria grow, leading to recurrent bronchitis and pneumonia.
Layers gas crosses: type I pneumocyte cytoplasm, fused basement membranes of alveolus and capillary, capillary endothelium.
It is under 1 micrometer thick over most of the surface.
Interstitial fibrosis or edema fluid thickens the barrier and slows diffusion.
Oxygen transfer suffers more than CO2 transfer, which shows as a low DLCO and desaturation with exercise.

charts.title: Changes along the airway
rows: Type I and type II pneumocytes

tricks.label: Cartilage and glands go together
tricks.text: Where you see cartilage, you see glands: trachea and bronchi. Lose the cartilage and the glands go too: bronchioles.

tricks.label: Type II does two things
tricks.text: Type II pneumocytes do two jobs: make surfactant and replace type I cells. Type I does one: get out of the way so gas can cross.

tricks.label: Gets thinner as you go down
tricks.text: Tall pseudostratified columnar, then simple columnar, then cuboidal, then flat type I cells. The lining flattens as the airway shifts from cleaning air to exchanging gas.

highYield: Terminal bronchioles have club cells and no goblet cells, cartilage, or glands.
Type II pneumocytes are the stem cells of the alveolus after injury.
Cilia: 9 plus 2 microtubules moved by dynein arms.
Kartagener syndrome: sinusitis, bronchiectasis, infertility, situs inversus.
Smoking causes squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium, a reversible change and a step toward squamous cell carcinoma.
Thickened blood-air barrier (fibrosis, edema) lowers DLCO.
True vocal folds have nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, so laryngeal cancer is mostly squamous cell carcinoma.
pitfalls: Type I cells cover most of the surface, yet type II cells are more numerous; do not confuse coverage with cell count.
False vocal folds (vestibular folds) have respiratory epithelium; true vocal folds have stratified squamous epithelium.
Cystic fibrosis makes mucus too thick to clear; primary ciliary dyskinesia leaves normal mucus with cilia that cannot move it.
Bronchioles have no cartilage; their patency depends on alveolar tethering and muscle tone, which is why emphysema causes expiratory collapse.

dumps.p: Make a table with rows for trachea, bronchus, bronchiole, terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, and alveolus. Add columns for epithelium, cartilage, glands, goblet cells, and the main cell types.
l: Trachea and bronchi: pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
Cartilage and glands stop at the bronchus
Bronchioles: no cartilage, no glands
Terminal bronchiole: simple cuboidal with club cells
Respiratory bronchiole: alveoli open off its wall
Alveolus: type I for exchange, type II for surfactant and repair
Smooth muscle is prominent in bronchioles

dumps.p: Draw a cross section of a cilium and label its parts. Then draw normal bronchial epithelium beside the epithelium of a long-term smoker, and explain why the smoker keeps getting infections.
l: Nine outer microtubule doublets around two central microtubules
Dynein arms use ATP to bend the cilium
Cilia move mucus up toward the pharynx
Smoker: squamous metaplasia with loss of cilia
Smoker: more goblet cells and larger submucosal glands
More mucus, less clearance, so bacteria stay and multiply
Dynein defects cause Kartagener syndrome

summary: The anatomy of the nose, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, and larynx: where the sinuses drain, where nosebleeds start, how the pharynx is divided, and which nerves move and feel the larynx. Exam questions use this anatomy to explain sinusitis, epistaxis, otitis media from big adenoids, hoarseness, and aspiration.

points: Each lateral wall has superior, middle, and inferior conchae; the space under each is its meatus.
Middle meatus (semilunar hiatus area): frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses.
Superior meatus: posterior ethmoid sinuses.
Sphenoethmoidal recess (above the superior concha): sphenoid sinus.
Inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct, which is why crying gives a runny nose.
Ethmoid cells sit behind a paper-thin orbital wall (lamina papyracea), so ethmoid sinusitis can spread to the orbit.
Largest sinus and the one most often infected.
Its ostium sits high on the medial wall, so the sinus cannot drain by gravity when upright.
Roots of the maxillary molars (and often premolars) lie just under its floor.
A tooth infection or extraction can open into the sinus and cause odontogenic sinusitis.
Kiesselbach area sits on the anterior nasal septum, where four arteries anastomose.
Arteries there: sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, and the septal branch of the superior labial.
About 90 percent of nosebleeds are anterior, from this area; usually mild, from nose picking, dry air, or trauma.
Posterior epistaxis comes from sphenopalatine branches; it bleeds more, runs down the throat, is harder to control, and is more common in older adults with hypertension.
Nasopharynx: behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate; holds the adenoids and the pharyngotympanic (eustachian) tube openings.
Oropharynx: from the soft palate to the tip of the epiglottis; holds the palatine and lingual tonsils.
Laryngopharynx: from the epiglottis to the lower border of the cricoid (about C6), where it becomes the esophagus; holds the piriform recesses.
Waldeyer ring: pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), tubal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and lingual tonsil.
Large adenoids block the choanae, causing mouth breathing and snoring, and block the eustachian tube, causing otitis media with effusion.
Unpaired cartilages: thyroid, cricoid (the only complete ring), epiglottis. Paired: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds.
Lateral cricoarytenoid and the arytenoid muscles adduct the folds; thyroarytenoid and vocalis relax and fine-tune them.
Cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to tense and lengthen the folds, raising pitch.
Superior laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) splits into the internal and external laryngeal nerves.
Internal laryngeal nerve: sensation above the vocal folds; it carries the afferent limb of the cough reflex.
External laryngeal nerve: motor to cricothyroid; injury (for example during thyroid surgery near the superior thyroid artery) gives a weak voice that cannot reach high pitch.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve: all other intrinsic muscles, and sensation below the folds.
The right recurrent nerve loops under the right subclavian artery; the left loops under the aortic arch, so it has a longer path and more places to be injured.
Unilateral recurrent nerve injury gives hoarseness; bilateral injury leaves both folds near the midline and causes stridor.
Loss of supraglottic sensation means food and secretions enter the larynx without a cough, so the patient aspirates.

tricks.label: LEGS
tricks.text: Kiesselbach area arteries: superior Labial (septal branch), anterior Ethmoidal, Greater palatine, Sphenopalatine.

tricks.label: Posterior opens the door
tricks.text: Posterior cricoarytenoid pulls the arytenoids apart to open the airway. It is the only abductor, so a paralyzed one leaves the fold sitting near the midline.

tricks.label: Most sinuses use the middle door
tricks.text: Frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid all drain into the middle meatus. Only the posterior ethmoid (superior meatus), the sphenoid (recess), and the tear duct (inferior meatus) use other doors.

highYield: Maxillary sinus is most often infected because its ostium is high on the medial wall.
An upper molar abscess can spread into the maxillary sinus.
Nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus.
Most nosebleeds come from Kiesselbach area on the anterior septum.
Enlarged adenoids cause mouth breathing, snoring, and otitis media.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only vocal fold abductor.
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch; an aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium, or left hilar lung tumor can cause hoarseness.
Internal laryngeal nerve damage removes the cough reflex above the folds and leads to aspiration.
pitfalls: Cricothyroid is the one intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve; the recurrent nerve supplies all the others.
Unilateral recurrent nerve palsy gives hoarseness; bilateral palsy gives stridor, since both folds sit near the midline.
Posterior ethmoid cells drain to the superior meatus, while anterior ethmoid cells drain to the middle meatus.
The right recurrent nerve hooks under the subclavian artery, the left under the aortic arch; chest disease affects the left side.

Sphenoid to the sphenoethmoidal recess
Nasolacrimal duct to the inferior meatus
Kiesselbach area on the anterior septum
Sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, superior labial

summary: The anatomy of the chest: where the lungs and pleura sit against the ribs, how the two lungs differ, what lies at each hilum, what fills each part of the mediastinum, and what passes through the diaphragm. Exam questions use this to place a needle, predict where aspirated material goes, localize a mass, explain shoulder pain, and recognize chylothorax.

points: Lower lung border: rib 6 at the midclavicular line, rib 8 at the midaxillary line, rib 10 at the paravertebral line.
Lower pleural border: rib 8, rib 10, rib 12 at the same lines, two ribs below the lung.
The gap between them is the costodiaphragmatic recess, where pleural fluid collects first.
Intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib.
So a thoracentesis needle goes just above the upper border of the rib below the chosen space.

notes.h: Right versus left lung and aspiration
points: Right lung: three lobes, separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures.
Left lung: two lobes, one oblique fissure, a lingula, and a cardiac notch for the heart.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, so aspirated material usually goes right.
Upright patient: aspirate settles in the right lower lobe (basal segments).
Supine patient: aspirate settles in the superior segment of the right lower lobe (and the posterior segment of the right upper lobe).
Each hilum holds a main bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, lymph nodes, and nerves.
Right pulmonary artery lies anterior to the right main bronchus.
Left pulmonary artery lies superior to the left main bronchus.
Pulmonary veins are the most anterior and inferior structures at both hila.
A plane through the sternal angle and the T4 to T5 disc separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum.
Superior: thymus, great vessels, superior vena cava, trachea, esophagus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves.
Anterior (sternum to pericardium): thymus remnant, fat, lymph nodes. Masses: thymoma, teratoma and other germ cell tumors, lymphoma, retrosternal thyroid.
Middle: pericardium, heart, roots of great vessels, phrenic nerves. Masses: enlarged lymph nodes, bronchogenic and pericardial cysts.
Posterior: esophagus, descending aorta, azygos veins, thoracic duct, vagus nerves, sympathetic trunks. Masses: neurogenic tumors (schwannoma, neurofibroma, neuroblastoma in children).
Parietal pleura is pain-sensitive: costal pleura and the peripheral diaphragm by intercostal nerves, mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura by the phrenic nerve.
Visceral pleura has autonomic supply only and does not feel sharp pain.
Pleuritis gives sharp pain on breathing only once the parietal pleura is involved.
Irritation of the central diaphragmatic pleura refers pain to the shoulder because the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) shares those cord segments with shoulder skin.
Irritation of the peripheral diaphragm refers pain to the lower chest wall and upper abdomen.
T8: inferior vena cava. T10: esophagus and both vagal trunks. T12: aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein.
Phrenic nerves (C3 to C5) give all motor supply and sensation to the central diaphragm.
Thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli in the upper abdomen and enters the chest through the aortic hiatus at T12.
It runs up the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and azygos vein, crosses to the left at about T5, and empties into the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.
Injury (surgery, trauma, tumor such as lymphoma) leaks lymph into the pleura: chylothorax, a milky fluid rich in triglycerides and chylomicrons.

tricks.label: I 8 10 Eggs At 12
tricks.text: "I ate ten eggs at twelve": IVC at T8, esophagus (with the vagal trunks) at T10, aorta (with the thoracic duct and azygos vein) at T12.

tricks.label: RALS
tricks.text: Right pulmonary artery is Anterior, Left pulmonary artery is Superior to its main bronchus.

tricks.label: The 4 Ts
tricks.text: Anterior mediastinal masses: Thymoma, Teratoma, Thyroid (retrosternal), and Terrible lymphoma.

tricks.label: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive
tricks.text: The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5, which also explains referred pain to the shoulder.

highYield: Pleura extends two ribs below the lung at every line: 8, 10, 12 versus 6, 8, 10.
Insert the thoracentesis needle just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle under the rib above.
Upright aspiration goes to the right lower lobe; supine aspiration goes to the superior segment of the right lower lobe.
Shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation travels by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).
Visceral pleura does not feel sharp pain; parietal pleura does.
Anterior mediastinal mass: think thymoma (with myasthenia gravis), teratoma, lymphoma, or thyroid.
Posterior mediastinal mass: think neurogenic tumor.
Milky pleural fluid high in triglycerides means a thoracic duct leak (chylothorax).
pitfalls: The neurovascular bundle runs under the lower border of each rib, so go over the top of the lower rib and never under the upper one.
Aspiration while lying down goes to the superior segment of the right lower lobe, which points backward, rather than the basal segments.
The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, not the esophageal hiatus.
Pleuritic pain means the parietal pleura is involved; disease confined to the lung and visceral pleura can be painless.
The thoracic duct ends on the left side, at the left venous angle, even though it starts on the right of the aorta.

summary: How blood and air move through the lungs: the low-pressure pulmonary circulation and the separate bronchial supply, how hypoxia constricts lung vessels, how gravity sets up West zones, and what controls airway and vascular resistance. Exam questions apply these ideas to pulmonary embolism, cor pulmonale, apical tuberculosis, and bronchoconstriction.

points: Pulmonary circulation carries the whole cardiac output at low pressure: about 25/8 mmHg, mean about 15 mmHg.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is about one tenth of systemic resistance.
Rising cardiac output recruits closed capillaries and widens open ones, so resistance falls as flow rises.
Bronchial arteries come from the thoracic aorta, directly or through an intercostal artery (systemic pressure), and feed the bronchi, connective tissue, and visceral pleura.
Some bronchial venous blood drains into the pulmonary veins, a small normal shunt.
Because lung tissue gets blood from both systems, most pulmonary emboli do not cause infarction.
Infarction becomes likely when bronchial flow is also poor, as in left heart failure; the infarct is wedge-shaped, hemorrhagic, and based on the pleura.
Low alveolar PO2 closes potassium channels in pulmonary arteriolar smooth muscle, which depolarizes it and lets calcium in, causing constriction.
This sends blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward well-ventilated ones and improves V/Q matching.
Systemic arterioles do the opposite: hypoxia dilates them to bring more blood to hungry tissue.
Generalized chronic hypoxia (COPD, sleep apnea, high altitude) constricts the whole pulmonary bed.
The result is pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy from lung disease: cor pulmonale.
Zone 1 (apex, only when alveolar pressure is high or arterial pressure low): alveolar > arterial > venous; no flow, so alveolar dead space.
Zone 2 (middle): arterial > alveolar > venous; flow depends on arterial minus alveolar pressure.
Zone 3 (base): arterial > venous > alveolar; flow depends on the usual arterial minus venous difference.
Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base, but perfusion rises more steeply.
So V/Q is highest at the apex (about 3) and lowest at the base (about 0.6); the whole lung averages about 0.8.
The apex has the highest alveolar PO2, which favors aerobic Mycobacterium tuberculosis in reactivation disease.
Conducting zone: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles; no gas exchange; anatomic dead space about 150 mL.
Respiratory zone: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs; gas exchange occurs here.
Medium-sized bronchi have the highest total resistance.
Small airways have tiny individual radii but are so many in parallel that their total cross-section is huge and their combined resistance is low.
Poiseuille law: resistance = 8 times viscosity times length divided by (pi times radius to the fourth power).
Halving the radius raises resistance 16-fold, so small changes in bronchial tone matter a lot.
Parasympathetic (vagal) acetylcholine on M3 receptors contracts airway smooth muscle and raises resistance.
Beta-2 stimulation by circulating epinephrine relaxes it and lowers resistance.
High lung volume pulls airways open by radial traction, lowering resistance; low lung volume narrows them.
In the large airways flow is turbulent, so resistance depends on gas density.
Denser gas (deep sea diving) raises resistance; a helium-oxygen mix lowers it.

notes.h: Pulmonary vascular resistance and lung volume
points: Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at functional residual capacity.
Low lung volume: extra-alveolar vessels lose radial traction and narrow, so resistance rises.
High lung volume: alveolar capillaries are stretched flat in the alveolar walls, so resistance rises.

Airway walls, connective tissue, visceral pleura
Bronchial veins to azygos system; some into pulmonary veins

tricks.label: Read the zones top to bottom
tricks.text: Put A for alveolar, a for arterial, v for venous. Zone 1 is A a v, zone 2 is a A v, zone 3 is a v A. Alveolar pressure slides down the list as you move down the lung.

tricks.label: Lungs think backwards about hypoxia
tricks.text: Systemic tissue that is short of oxygen calls for more blood. Lung tissue that is short of oxygen sends blood elsewhere, because that alveolus cannot load it.

tricks.label: Radius to the fourth
tricks.text: Halve the radius and resistance goes up 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16 times. Double it and resistance drops to one sixteenth.

highYield: Dual blood supply means most pulmonary emboli do not infarct the lung.
Hypoxic vasoconstriction in the lung is the opposite of the systemic response.
Chronic hypoxia leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
V/Q is highest at the apex; reactivation TB likes the apex for its high PO2.
Both ventilation and perfusion are highest at the base.
Medium-sized bronchi give the most airway resistance.
Resistance varies with 1 over radius to the fourth power.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at FRC.
pitfalls: The base has a low V/Q even though it gets the most ventilation, because perfusion rises even more there.
Small airways look like they should resist most, yet their parallel arrangement keeps total resistance low; disease there is silent until advanced.
Zone 1 does not exist in a healthy upright lung; it appears with low arterial pressure or high alveolar pressure.
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises at both low and high lung volumes, by different mechanisms.

dumps.p: Draw an upright lung divided into zones 1, 2, and 3. In each zone, write the order of alveolar, arterial, and venous pressure. Beside the lung, draw how ventilation, perfusion, and V/Q change from apex to base.
l: Zone 1: alveolar > arterial > venous, no flow
Zone 2: arterial > alveolar > venous
Zone 3: arterial > venous > alveolar
Ventilation and perfusion both rise toward the base
Perfusion rises more steeply
V/Q about 3 at the apex, about 0.6 at the base
High apical PO2 favors reactivation TB

dumps.p: Trace what happens from low alveolar oxygen in one region, then in the whole lung, ending at the right ventricle. Contrast it with what hypoxia does to a systemic arteriole.
l: Low alveolar PO2 closes K channels in pulmonary arteriolar muscle
Depolarization and calcium entry cause constriction
Local effect: blood diverted to better-ventilated alveoli
Global chronic hypoxia constricts the whole pulmonary bed
Pulmonary hypertension develops
Right ventricular hypertrophy, cor pulmonale
Systemic arterioles dilate in hypoxia

summary: How air gets in and out of the lungs: lung volumes, minute and alveolar ventilation, the elastic forces of lung and chest wall, spirometry, and the brainstem and chemoreceptor control of breathing. Exam questions ask students to calculate ventilation, read flow-volume loops, predict the response to high CO2 or low O2, and sort out the sleep-related breathing disorders.

points: Tidal volume (TV) about 500 mL; inspiratory reserve (IRV) about 3000 mL; expiratory reserve (ERV) about 1100 mL; residual volume (RV) about 1200 mL.
Functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV, about 2300 mL: the volume left after a normal breath out.
Vital capacity (VC) = IRV + TV + ERV, about 4600 mL; total lung capacity (TLC) = VC + RV, about 5800 mL.
Spirometry cannot measure RV, so it misses FRC and TLC too. Helium dilution measures gas that communicates with the airways; body plethysmography (Boyle law) also counts trapped gas.

notes.h: Minute ventilation, alveolar ventilation, dead space
points: Minute ventilation = TV x respiratory rate; 500 mL x 12 = 6 L/min.
Alveolar ventilation = (TV minus dead space) x rate; (500 minus 150) x 12 = 4.2 L/min.
Bohr equation: VD/VT = (PaCO2 minus mixed expired PCO2) / PaCO2; normal is about 0.3.
Physiologic dead space = anatomic dead space + alveolar dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli).
Rapid shallow breathing (250 mL x 24) keeps minute ventilation at 6 L/min but drops alveolar ventilation to 2.4 L/min.
PaCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation, so hypoventilation raises PaCO2.
Compliance is change in volume per change in pressure. The lung recoils inward and the chest wall springs outward; at FRC these forces balance.
That balance makes intrapleural pressure about minus 5 cmH2O at FRC.
Law of Laplace: collapsing pressure = 2 x surface tension / radius, so small alveoli would empty into large ones.
Surfactant lowers surface tension, and more so in small alveoli where it is concentrated, which stabilizes them, raises compliance, and keeps fluid out of alveoli.
Obstructive: FEV1 falls more than FVC, FEV1/FVC below 0.7, TLC normal or high, RV high from air trapping; expiratory limb scooped.
Restrictive: FEV1 and FVC both fall, FEV1/FVC normal or high, TLC low; loop is small and shifted to lower volumes.
DLCO separates restrictive causes: low in interstitial lung disease, normal in chest wall or neuromuscular causes.
Fixed upper airway obstruction (tracheal stenosis): both inspiratory and expiratory limbs flatten into plateaus.
Variable extrathoracic obstruction (vocal fold paralysis) flattens the inspiratory limb; variable intrathoracic obstruction flattens the expiratory limb.
Dorsal respiratory group (nucleus tractus solitarius region of the medulla): drives inspiration and receives input from CN IX and X.
Ventral respiratory group (medulla): quiet in normal breathing; fires both inspiratory and expiratory neurons during forced breathing.
Pneumotaxic center (upper pons): limits inspiration, which shortens each breath and raises the rate.
Apneustic center (lower pons): prolongs inspiration; unchecked, it causes long inspiratory gasps (apneusis).
Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: stretch receptors in the airways send signals by the vagus to stop inspiration when the lung is overinflated; it matters most in infants and at large tidal volumes.
Central chemoreceptors (ventral medulla) respond to hydrogen ions in CSF.
CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier easily and forms H+ in poorly buffered CSF; blood H+ crosses poorly.
Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid bodies (CN IX) and aortic bodies (CN X); they respond mainly to PaO2 below about 60 mmHg, and also to PaCO2 and H+.
The carotid bodies are the main sensors of arterial H+, so they drive the hyperventilation of metabolic acidosis.
Ventilation rises steeply and steadily with PaCO2, but changes little with falling PaO2 until it drops below about 60 mmHg.
In chronic CO2 retention, CSF bicarbonate rises and central drive blunts; high-flow oxygen can then raise PaCO2, mostly by worsening V/Q matching and the Haldane effect.

Obstructive sleep apnea: the pharynx collapses during sleep while chest and abdominal effort continue; risks are obesity, large tonsils, and a small jaw; snoring, daytime sleepiness, and morning headache are typical.
Central sleep apnea: no respiratory effort during the pauses; seen with heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes breathing), opioids, and brainstem injury.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome: BMI 30 or more with daytime PaCO2 above 45 mmHg and no other cause.
Repeated nighttime hypoxia causes hypoxic vasoconstriction, so pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale follow.
Hypoxia also raises erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia.

tricks.label: Capacities are sums
tricks.text: Any capacity is two or more volumes added together. Any capacity that includes RV (FRC, TLC) needs helium dilution or plethysmography.

tricks.label: Shallow wastes air
tricks.text: Dead space is a fixed tax of about 150 mL on every breath. Small breaths pay the same tax, so more of each breath is wasted.

tricks.label: Ratio tells the family
tricks.text: FEV1/FVC low means obstructive. FEV1/FVC normal or high with small volumes means restrictive. Then DLCO tells you whether the problem is in the lung or outside it.

highYield: Alveolar ventilation = (TV minus dead space) x rate.
Rapid shallow breathing lowers alveolar ventilation and raises PaCO2 at the same minute ventilation.
Spirometry cannot measure RV, FRC, or TLC.
Obstructive: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 and high TLC; restrictive: normal ratio and low TLC.
Fixed upper airway obstruction flattens both limbs of the flow-volume loop.
Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF H+ from CO2; peripheral ones respond to PaO2 below 60 mmHg.
Surfactant prevents small alveoli from collapsing, as Laplace law predicts they otherwise would.
Sleep apnea and obesity hypoventilation lead to pulmonary hypertension and secondary polycythemia.
pitfalls: FEV1 and FVC both fall in restrictive disease, so the ratio stays normal or rises; do not call a low FEV1 obstruction without checking the ratio.
Peripheral chemoreceptors sense PaO2, not oxygen content, so they do not fire much in anemia or CO poisoning.
Obstructive sleep apnea has continued effort against a closed airway; central sleep apnea has no effort at all.
Emphysema increases compliance; fibrosis decreases it.
Hering-Breuer stops inspiration when the lung is overinflated; it is weak at normal adult tidal volumes.

dumps.p: Draw a spirogram and label all four volumes and four capacities with normal values. Then draw a normal flow-volume loop, an obstructive loop, a restrictive loop, and a fixed upper airway obstruction loop on the same axes.
l: TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1100, RV 1200 mL
FRC = ERV + RV; VC = IRV + TV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV
RV, FRC, and TLC cannot be measured by spirometry
Obstructive loop: scooped expiratory limb, shifted to higher volumes
Restrictive loop: small, shifted to lower volumes, ratio preserved
Fixed upper airway obstruction: flat inspiratory and expiratory limbs
FEV1/FVC below 0.7 means obstruction

dumps.p: Draw the brainstem and label the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups and the pontine centers. Add the central and peripheral chemoreceptors with their nerves and the stimulus each senses. Then explain what happens to breathing when PaCO2 rises and when PaO2 falls to 50 mmHg.
l: Dorsal group: inspiration, input from CN IX and X
Ventral group: forced breathing, both inspiration and expiration
Pneumotaxic center limits inspiration; apneustic center prolongs it
Central chemoreceptors: CSF H+ formed from CO2
Carotid bodies by CN IX, aortic bodies by CN X
Peripheral chemoreceptors fire strongly when PaO2 is below about 60 mmHg
Rising PaCO2 increases ventilation steeply and steadily
Hering-Breuer reflex stops inspiration by vagal stretch receptors

summary: How oxygen gets from the alveolus into blood and out to tissues: the alveolar gas equation and A-a gradient, the five causes of hypoxemia, dead space versus shunt, diffusion, the four types of hypoxia, and adaptation to altitude. Exam questions give an arterial blood gas and ask students to find the cause, predict the response to oxygen, or explain altitude illness.

notes.h: Alveolar gas equation and A-a gradient
points: PAO2 = FiO2 x (Patm minus 47) minus PaCO2 / 0.8.
At sea level on room air: 0.21 x (760 minus 47) = about 150; 150 minus 40/0.8 = about 100 mmHg.
A-a gradient = PAO2 minus PaO2; normal is about 5 to 15 mmHg in young adults and rises with age.
A normal gradient points outside the lung (low inspired O2 or low ventilation); a widened gradient points to diffusion, V/Q mismatch, or shunt.
Low inspired O2 (altitude): normal A-a gradient, corrects with O2.
Hypoventilation (opioids, neuromuscular weakness): high PaCO2, normal A-a gradient, corrects with O2.
Diffusion limitation (fibrosis): widened gradient, corrects with O2.
V/Q mismatch (COPD, asthma, pneumonia, embolism): widened gradient, corrects with O2; the most common cause.
Right-to-left shunt: widened gradient and poor correction with 100 percent O2, because shunted blood never meets the added oxygen.
Dead space: ventilation without perfusion, V/Q approaches infinity; alveolar gas looks like inspired air. Example: pulmonary embolism.

Shunt: perfusion without ventilation, V/Q = 0; blood leaves with mixed venous gas (PO2 about 40, PCO2 about 46 mmHg). Examples: airway obstruction, alveoli filled with pus in pneumonia or with fluid in edema, atelectasis.
Shunt lowers PaO2; PaCO2 usually stays normal or low because the remaining units can blow off extra CO2 but cannot add extra O2 to blood that is already saturated.
Dead space alone would raise PaCO2, but the patient usually hyperventilates, so PaCO2 is often low in embolism.
Embolism also lowers PaO2 because blood diverted to the remaining vessels overperfuses those alveoli, creating low V/Q units.
Fick law: gas transfer = (surface area / thickness) x diffusion constant x partial pressure difference.
Thicker barrier (fibrosis, edema) or smaller area (emphysema, lung resection) means slower transfer.
Perfusion-limited gas (N2O, O2 at rest): equilibrates early in the capillary, so only more blood flow raises uptake.
Diffusion-limited gas (CO; O2 in fibrosis or during strenuous exercise at altitude): does not equilibrate before blood leaves the capillary.
Resting red cells spend about 0.75 s in the capillary and O2 equilibrates in about 0.25 s, leaving a safety margin that disease and exercise use up.
DLCO is low in emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis, and normal in chronic bronchitis and asthma.
Hypoxemia means low PaO2 in arterial blood; hypoxia means too little O2 reaching or used by tissue.
O2 content = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2); normal about 20 mL O2/dL.
Hypoxemic hypoxia: low PaO2, low SaO2, low content.
Anemic hypoxia: normal PaO2 and SaO2, low content from low hemoglobin.
Carbon monoxide: normal PaO2, low true SaO2 by co-oximetry (pulse oximetry reads falsely normal), low content, and a left-shifted curve.
Circulatory hypoxia (shock, heart failure, arterial blockage): normal PaO2, SaO2, and content, but low flow delivers too little.
Histotoxic hypoxia (cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase): normal PaO2, SaO2, and content; tissues cannot use O2, so venous O2 stays high and lactate rises.
Lower barometric pressure lowers inspired and alveolar PO2, giving hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient.
Peripheral chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation, which lowers PaCO2 and causes respiratory alkalosis.
Over days the kidneys excrete bicarbonate, correcting pH and allowing ventilation to rise further.
Erythropoietin rises, raising hemoglobin over weeks; 2,3-BPG rises, shifting the curve right to help unloading.
Generalized hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causes pulmonary hypertension and, over time, right ventricular hypertrophy.
Acute mountain sickness: headache, nausea, fatigue, poor sleep within hours of a fast ascent, usually above about 2500 m.
High altitude pulmonary edema: uneven vasoconstriction overloads the less constricted capillaries, which leak; dyspnea at rest and cough.
High altitude cerebral edema: confusion and ataxia; it can progress to coma. Descent and oxygen are the key responses to both edemas.

charts.title: Causes of hypoxemia
rows: Pneumonia with filled alveoli, ARDS, atelectasis

tricks.label: Gradient sorts the causes
tricks.text: Normal A-a gradient: the problem is outside the lung (thin air or too little breathing). Then PaCO2 splits them: high means hypoventilation, normal or low means altitude.

tricks.label: Shunt ignores oxygen
tricks.text: Blood that never passes a ventilated alveolus never sees the extra oxygen. If 100 percent O2 barely moves the PaO2, think shunt.

tricks.label: Which number is low
tricks.text: Ask which of PaO2, SaO2, and content is low. All three low: hypoxemic. PaO2 normal but content low: anemia (SaO2 normal) or CO (true SaO2 low). None low: circulatory or histotoxic, then look at venous O2.

highYield: PAO2 = FiO2 x (Patm minus 47) minus PaCO2/0.8, about 100 mmHg at sea level.
Normal A-a gradient with hypoxemia means hypoventilation or low inspired O2.
Shunt is the hypoxemia that does not correct with 100 percent oxygen.
Pulmonary embolism is the classic dead space problem; pneumonia filling alveoli is the classic shunt.
CO is diffusion-limited; N2O and resting O2 are perfusion-limited.
DLCO is low in emphysema and fibrosis, normal in asthma and chronic bronchitis.
Cyanide: normal PaO2, high venous O2, lactic acidosis.
Altitude: hyperventilation, respiratory alkalosis, renal bicarbonate loss, more EPO and 2,3-BPG.
pitfalls: Pulse oximetry reads near normal in CO poisoning because it cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin; co-oximetry shows the true low SaO2.
Anemia lowers O2 content but leaves PaO2 and SaO2 normal.
Shunt rarely raises PaCO2 because healthy units can blow off extra CO2; it is oxygen that cannot be made up.

Pure hypoventilation gives a high PaCO2 with a normal gradient; a high PaCO2 with a widened gradient means lung disease is present, such as severe COPD with V/Q mismatch, alone or on top of hypoventilation.
Altitude hypoxemia has a normal A-a gradient; HAPE adds a widened gradient once edema develops.

dumps.p: Write the alveolar gas equation and calculate PAO2 at sea level on room air with a PaCO2 of 40 mmHg. Then build a flow chart that sorts the five causes of hypoxemia using the A-a gradient, PaCO2, and the response to 100 percent oxygen.
l: PAO2 = FiO2 x (Patm minus 47) minus PaCO2/0.8
0.21 x 713 = about 150; minus 50 = about 100 mmHg
Normal gradient with high PaCO2: hypoventilation
Normal gradient with normal or low PaCO2: low inspired O2
Widened gradient that corrects with O2: V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation
Widened gradient that does not correct: shunt
V/Q mismatch is the most common cause

dumps.p: Make a table of hypoxemic, anemic, circulatory, and histotoxic hypoxia, plus carbon monoxide poisoning. For each, write PaO2, SaO2, O2 content, venous O2, and one cause.
l: Hypoxemic: all three low
Anemic: PaO2 and SaO2 normal, content low
CO: PaO2 normal, true SaO2 low, content low, pulse oximetry misleading
Circulatory: all normal, delivery low from poor flow
Histotoxic: all normal, venous O2 high
Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase and causes lactic acidosis
O2 content = 1.34 x Hb x SaO2 + 0.003 x PaO2
